source: Wang et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning - method
finding: Sample many reasoning paths with temperature, top-k or nucleus sampling. Parse the final answer of each path. Pick the most frequent answer (marginalise out the path). It needs no training and no extra model.
numbers: Sampling: UL2-20B and LaMDA-137B T=0.5 k=40; PaLM-540B T=0.7 k=40; GPT-3 T=0.7. Default 40 paths, averaged over 10 runs.
quote: Self-consistency first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only the greedy one
limits: Needs a fixed, parseable final answer (the 'The answer is X' format). Free-form answers cannot be voted by exact match.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S3 GENERATE plus a code-run S7 SELECT: the program counts answers, the model never judges.

source: Wang et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning - arithmetic results (Table 2)
finding: Voting beats greedy chain of thought on all arithmetic sets and all four models. The gain grows with model scale up to GPT-3 and LaMDA, and stays large for the biggest models on hard sets.
limits: Gain is small when the base is near the ceiling (AddSub PaLM 91.9 -> 93.7). Small models gain only +3 to +6.
agent_relevance: Expect the biggest vote gain where single-sample accuracy is middling (about 30-80%), not near 100% or near 0%.

source: Wang et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning - commonsense and symbolic (Table 3)
finding: Gains are smaller on commonsense than on arithmetic. On out-of-distribution symbolic tasks the vote helps large models but not the tiny one.
limits: If the model cannot do the task at all, voting adds nothing (zero base accuracy stays zero).
agent_relevance: Voting cannot rescue a task the model never solves; use it only where some samples are right.

source: Wang et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning - aggregation rules (Table 1)
finding: Plain majority vote equals the best probability-weighted vote. Raw model probabilities barely separate paths, so weighting adds nothing. Averaging by normalised score is far worse.
numbers: PaLM-540B GSM8K: majority vote 74.4; weighted sum normalised 74.1; weighted sum unnormalised 59.9; weighted average normalised 22.1; unnormalised 56.3; greedy 56.5. AQuA: vote 48.3, normalised sum 48.0, unnormalised 38.2.
quote: the normalized conditional probabilities are quite close to each other
limits: Paper reads the near-equal path probabilities as a sign the model is poorly calibrated.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: use a code count, not model likelihood. Model scores add no signal here.

source: Wang et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning - sample and rank, beam search, ensembles (Fig 3, Tables 6, 7, 11)
finding: Voting beats sample-and-rank by likelihood, beam search, and prompt ensembles. Beam search loses because it lacks diversity. Prompt-set and prompt-order ensembles give much smaller gains.
numbers: UL2-20B AQuA: beam search top beam falls 23.6 (1 beam) -> 10.2 (40 beams); sampling vote rises 19.7 -> 26.9 (40 paths). LaMDA-137B GSM8K: CoT 17.1, 3-prompt ensemble 18.6, 40 permutations 19.2, self-consistency 27.7. PaLM GSM8K: 40 prompt sets 58.9, 40 permutations 59.6, SC 74.4, SC + 40 prompt sets 75.4, SC + permutations 73.8.
limits: Beam search is an optimiser and drifts to one mode; sampling is needed for diversity.
agent_relevance: Diversity comes from sampling the thought, not from re-prompting. Stacking prompt variants on top of sampling gives about +1 or none.

source: Wang et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning - robustness, consistency as confidence, NLP tasks
finding: The gain holds over temperature, top-k and nucleus settings, with imperfect prompts, and with zero-shot CoT. Agreement rate tracks accuracy, so it works as an uncertainty signal. Where CoT hurts versus no rationale, voting repairs it.
numbers: LaMDA GSM8K imperfect-CoT prompt 14.9 -> 23.4 with 40 paths; equation prompt 5.0 -> 6.5; PaLM zero-shot CoT 43.0 -> 69.2 (+26.2). Fig 5: consistency % correlates with accuracy on GSM8K. PaLM NLP (Table 5): ANLI-R1 CoT 68.8 -> SC 78.5; e-SNLI 81.0 -> 88.4; RTE 79.1 -> 86.3; BoolQ 74.2 -> 78.4; HotpotQA EM 28.9 -> 33.8. Standard prompting beat CoT on ANLI-R1 (69.1), e-SNLI (85.8), RTE (84.8).
quote: self-consistency confers some ability for the model to know when it doesn't know
limits: Paper says consistency is correlated with accuracy and gives no calibration error number. Gain saturates quickly; authors suggest 5 or 10 paths as a start. Cost is a stated limitation.
agent_relevance: Agreement rate is a free confidence signal for the doubt trigger (G1). It is a hint only (G4).

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models
finding: The base method that voting sits on. Eight chain-of-thought examples lift PaLM-540B to state of the art on GSM8K, above finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier. Gains are larger on harder problems and negligible on one-step ones.
numbers: Greedy CoT PaLM-540B GSM8K 56.5 (value used in Wang et al. Table 2). On SingleOp, the easiest MAWPS subset, gains were negative or very small. On GSM8K performance more than doubled for the largest GPT and PaLM models.
quote: performance more than doubled for the largest GPT and PaLM models
limits: Emergent only in models around 100B parameters or more.
agent_relevance: Voting needs a per-sample chain; this is the sample-generation layer of S3.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training verifiers to solve math word problems
finding: Predecessor and rival to voting. Train a verifier, sample 100 solutions, take the top-ranked. Verifier beats finetuning once data is large enough. A majority vote over the top verifier-ranked answers adds a bit more.
numbers: GSM8K 8.5K problems. 100 completions per problem; test@100 sampled at T=0.7, test@1 at T=0. Voting among top verifier-ranked: with 100 samples best to let top 3-5 vote; with 3200 samples best to let top 30 vote. Verifier performance rises to 400 samples then falls.
quote: the benefits of search are eventually outweighed by the risk of finding adversarial solutions that fool the verifier
limits: Verification did not help at low dataset size (overfitting). Beyond 400 samples the verifier is fooled by adversarial solutions. A large generator with a small verifier beat a small generator with a large verifier.
agent_relevance: Shows a learned scorer can be gamed by more samples; a code-run vote has no such weak point but ignores quality. Supports G5 caution on model judges.

source: Li et al. (2022/ACL 2023) DiVeRSe: Making LLMs better reasoners with step-aware verifier - headline
finding: Three add-ons to voting: diverse prompts, a verifier weighting the votes, and step-level scoring. Reaches 82.3 on GSM8K with code-davinci-002, above 76.7 for self-consistency and 74.4 for PaLM self-consistency.
numbers: code-davinci-002 GSM8K (Table 1): self-consistency 76.7, DiVeRSe 82.3 (+5.6). Diverse prompts (5 prompts x 20 samples) vs 1 prompt x 100 samples, both majority vote: GSM8K 80.0 vs 76.7 (code-davinci-002); 61.3 vs 58.2 (text-davinci-002).
limits: Needs training data and a trained verifier. Prompt diversity gives +3 here, against about +1 or none for prompt ensembles in Wang et al.
agent_relevance: Prompt diversity might add a little over pure sampling, but G4 bars persona or strategy voters on single-answer problems; test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Li et al. (2022) DiVeRSe - verifier ablation (Table 5)
finding: Weighting votes by a verifier helps weaker models more than strong ones. The verifier used alone can lose to plain voting.
numbers: GSM8K davinci: voting 21.3, verifier 27.0, voting verifier 30.6. text-davinci-002: 61.3 / 62.7 / 68.9. code-davinci-002: 80.0 / 65.9 / 82.3 (verifier alone far below voting). CLUTRR code-davinci-002: 43.8 / 95.9 / 95.9.
limits: Task dependent: on inductive CLUTRR the verifier dominates the vote.
agent_relevance: A learned weight is worth it only where it beats the vote alone; check at equal tokens (G7).

source: Fu et al. (2022/ICLR 2023) Complexity-based prompting for multi-step reasoning
finding: Vote only over the K sampled chains with the most reasoning steps. This beats voting over all chains. Voting over the simplest K chains is worse than voting over all.
numbers: N=50 samples, K=10 to 50 (K=50 is plain self-consistency). Code-davinci-002 GSM8K: Complex CoT 82.6 -> plus vote over complex 82.9; text-davinci-002 Complex CoT 71.5 -> 72.6.
limits: Gain from complex-chain voting is small (+0.3 to +1.1) on top of complex prompts. Step count is a proxy that holds only where longer chains mean more careful work.
agent_relevance: A cheap code-computed filter (step count) before the vote fits S7 where code selects. Test against length bias (G5).

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling once a clear majority exists, using a Beta or Dirichlet stopping rule. This cuts samples with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs, max 40 samples, T=0.7. Up to 7.9x fewer samples, average accuracy drop under 0.1%. Math 3.3x fewer (0.1% drop); commonsense 2.9x (0.2%); symbolic 3.8x; code 2.4x. GPT-3.5-turbo 4.4x fewer (under 0.2% drop); Vicuna-13B 1.9x. At equal average cost, up to 5 points above fixed-budget SC.
limits: Savings are largest on easy items where answers agree fast; hard items still need the full budget.
agent_relevance: Gives the stop rule for S3: stop generating when the vote is lopsided, spend more when it is split. Matches G1 (act on a signal).

source: Chen et al. (2023) Universal self-consistency for LLM generation
finding: Where answers are free text and cannot be matched, ask the model to pick the most consistent response among the samples. It matches exact-match voting on math and execution-based voting on code.
numbers: PaLM 2-L GSM8K greedy 85.7, random sample 82.9, SC 90.4, USC 90.2; MATH 30.8 / 28.0 / 37.9 / 37.4. gpt-3.5-turbo GSM8K 73.4 / 68.5 / 78.5 / 77.8; MATH 33.2 / 26.3 / 38.0 / 38.1. Code (gpt-3.5): ARCADE SC-Exec 45.6 vs USC 45.5; BIRD-SQL SC-Exec (fuzzy) 30.3 vs USC 30.1.
limits: The model does the choosing, so authorship, order and length bias can enter. The number of samples is capped by context length. A random pick was worse than greedy.
agent_relevance: A model-judged vote conflicts with G5 (code selects). Use only for free-form output, with the judge blind to authorship and order.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling - coverage
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) keeps rising over four orders of magnitude of samples. With a code verifier this is real accuracy. Without one, majority voting and reward models stall.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct MATH: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. SWE-bench Lite DeepSeek-Coder-V2 15.9% (1 sample) to 56% (250), above the single-sample state of the art 43%. Gemma-2B CodeContests 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000.
quote: common methods for picking from a sample collection (majority voting and reward models) plateau beyond several hundred samples
limits: Reward model was ArmoRM-Llama3-8B; one model family and mostly math for the voting comparison.
agent_relevance: Core boundary: voting works only while the right answer is the mode. Where a code check exists (tests, held-out example), use it instead of a vote (G3, G5).

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys - why voting plateaus
finding: Majority vote cannot gain from rare correct samples, because they do not change the most common answer. The gap between coverage and voted accuracy grows with the sample count.
numbers: Reward-model best-of-N plateaus near 100 samples. Coverage exceeds 95% while vote stays near 41% for Llama-3-8B on MATH.
quote: the occurrence of rare, correct solutions does not affect the most common answer
limits: Single setup; the paper gives the reason as intuition, not a proof.
agent_relevance: Argues for a code-run checker over a bigger vote when the sample count is large.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: The best way to spend test-time samples depends on question difficulty. Compute-optimal allocation beats plain best-of-N by more than 4x in compute. On easy items beam search over a process verifier gets worse as budget grows.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S*. Compute-optimal is more than 4x more efficient than best-of-N. A smaller model with test-time compute can beat a 14x larger one in FLOPs-matched tests where the small model has some success. Beam search (width 4) vs best-of-N: worse on levels 1-2 as budget rises, better on levels 3-4, no method helps on level 5.
quote: on the most difficult questions (level 5), no method makes much meaningful progress
limits: Difficulty is model-specific and costs compute to estimate. Gains shrink on the hardest questions. Mostly about verifier search, not plain voting.
agent_relevance: Sampling budget should depend on measured difficulty: small for agreed-easy items, larger for split ones.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Are more LLM calls all you need? Towards scaling laws of compound inference systems
finding: Theory and data show majority voting can get worse with more samples. More calls help easy queries and hurt hard ones, so a mixed task can peak and then fall.
numbers: Vote and Filter-Vote on MMLU-Physics: easy queries (53%) improve with more calls, hard queries (47%) degrade (Fig 2). An analytical scaling model, fit from a few samples, predicts the best number of calls. On hard queries a wrong answer is the mode, so votes converge on it.
limits: Binary easy/hard split is a simplification. Tested on a few language tasks, mostly multiple choice.
agent_relevance: Direct rule for the harness: if the first samples are split and the top answer has a low share, more votes may lock in a wrong answer; route to a check, not more votes (G3, G4).

source: Condorcet jury theorem (1785) as the formal base of voting
finding: If voters are independent and each beats chance on a two-way choice, the majority is right with probability rising to 1 as voters grow. If each is below chance, the majority gets worse. Not opened this session; stated from memory.
numbers: No numbers claimed.
limits: Needs independence. Samples from one model are correlated, so the limit is below 1, and when the model's top answer is wrong, voting converges to wrong.
agent_relevance: Formal reason for G4: same-model samples are not independent, so agreement is a hint. Chen 2024 and Brown 2024 match this pattern empirically.

source: Fu et al. (2022) Complexity-based prompting - prompt side of the result
finding: Choosing prompt examples with more reasoning steps raises accuracy, and the vote then adds on top. Extra gain is mostly from the prompt, not the vote filter.
numbers: Average +5.3 on GPT-3 and +6.2 on Codex across tasks, up to +18 (MathQA Complex CoT 47.3, +18.0 over baseline). GSM8K text-davinci-002: handcrafted 64.0, random 62.0, complex 71.5.
limits: Confounders such as case count or prompt length were checked (Table 8), step count was the main factor at moderate per-step length.
agent_relevance: Few-shot example choice matters at least as much as the vote; keep S3 prompts fixed when comparing vote rules.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency - stopping rules compared
finding: Beta and Dirichlet stopping beat a simple majority-count stopping rule. The stopping check costs almost nothing compared with an LLM call.
numbers: Stopping check time about 0.03 ms vs about 100 ms per sample (Table 2 timing). Majority-based stopping almost always underperforms Beta and Dirichlet at the same average cost.
limits: Beta uses only the top two counts; assumes samples are exchangeable draws, which same-model samples only approximate.
agent_relevance: Code-side stop rule: a few lines, no model call, fits the program-decides rule.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency - cost and stated limits
finding: Cost is the main stated limitation. Most of the gain comes early, so a few paths already help.
numbers: Typical jobs: 1 to 4 hours per 1,000 examples on UL2 and LaMDA-137B TPUs, 2 to 12 hours on PaLM-540B. Paper advises 5 or 10 paths as a starting point; gains saturate (Fig 2).
limits: Authors also note that paths can be nonsensical (StrategyQA example with wrong population numbers) so a correct vote can sit on bad reasoning.
agent_relevance: Budget the vote at 5 to 10 samples first, and widen only on a split vote.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) - sampled coverage vs overfitting
finding: A model needs diverse samples to be useful for selection. Finetuning for more epochs raises single-sample accuracy but cuts the diversity of 100 samples.
numbers: 6B model: test@1 improves over epochs while test@100 (T=0.7) degrades much more sharply; test@100 peaks within the first few epochs. Authors choose a model with good coverage to train verifiers.
limits: Fine-tuned models only; prompted models behave differently.
agent_relevance: Diversity is a resource: sharpening or low-temperature sampling shrinks what a vote can use.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency - scale effect and zero-gain case
finding: Gain rises with model size from UL2-20B to LaMDA-137B and GPT-3, but is smaller for the smallest model, because the skill (arithmetic) is not there yet.
numbers: GSM8K gains: UL2-20B +3.2, LaMDA-137B +10.6, GPT-3 code-davinci-001 +8.8, PaLM-540B +17.9, code-davinci-002 +17.9. Equation-style paths gave smaller gains than natural language (5.0 -> 6.5) because short paths leave less room for diverse sampling.
limits: Gains need diverse paths; short or templated reasoning cuts diversity and so the vote gain.
agent_relevance: Keep the sampled thought long enough to differ between samples; very short outputs give a vote nothing to vote on.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-consistency - weak-prompt repair
finding: With a deliberately flawed prompt (numbers in the examples swapped for random ones), the greedy answer drops but a 40-path vote recovers beyond the clean greedy level.
numbers: LaMDA-137B GSM8K: clean-prompt greedy 17.1, imperfect-prompt greedy 14.9, imperfect prompt + 40 paths 23.4.
limits: One model and one set.
agent_relevance: The vote hides some prompt errors; it can also hide a defect we would want to see, so log vote splits.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys - model choice under fixed budget
finding: At equal compute, a smaller model with many samples can beat a larger model with few samples on some sets (for example MATH), when a verifier can pick the right sample.
numbers: Abstract states coverage scales over four orders of magnitude; text says on some datasets such as MATH coverage is maximised with a smaller model at fixed cost.
limits: Exact FLOPs-matched numbers were not copied; claim is from the paper text only.
agent_relevance: Many cheap samples plus a code check can beat one expensive pass; test against the plain model at equal tokens (G7).
